tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: SearchPlugins

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

You have access to Blender tools to interact with a Blender scene directly.

NEVER assume missing values - inspect the scene first.
Do not destructively modify objects without confirmation.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).
    Consult when writing or debugging `bpy` code: operator signatures, type
    properties, enum values, etc.
  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

53	
54	**A person.** Two independent sources tying the person to the role. If a namesake exists, say which one you rejected and why.
55

57

59	# <note code> <title> (agent: <model>, 2026-11-13)
60	
61	## Digest
62	(400 words at most: the 12 facts that matter most for deciding what to build tonight, each with its fact ID; 3 surprises; anything that contradicts the starting leads in section 7.)
63	
64	## Findings
65	(grouped under the key questions in your task)
66	
67	## NOT FOUND / NOT SEARCHED
68	
69	Searches used: N
70	```

73	
74	The coordinator's unverified starting ideas. Look for evidence against them as hard as evidence for them.
75	
76	1. Programmes that change the treatment from home readings (dose titration, protocol steps) improve outcomes; monitoring and reminders alone mostly do not.
77	2. In India the binding limit is the prescriber's time and the gap between visits, so the workable design keeps a doctor or health worker approving each change while software does the reading, the protocol logic and the drafting.
78	3. Candidate loops: (a) home blood-pressure readings driving a stepwise medicine protocol; (b) fasting-glucose readings driving insulin dose changes in type 2 diabetes; (c) an inhaler or breathing sensor plus air-quality data adapting an asthma or COPD plan; (d) phone-camera and pulse-sensor rehabilitation that adapts each session.
79	4. The durable advantage is outcome data, clinical validation and distribution, not the app.
80	5. The honest regulatory route is decision support with clinician sign-off first; autonomous dosing needs a licence later.
81	
82	## 8. Style
83	
84	Dense, factual, plain words, short sentences. No marketing language. No em dashes. Rupees with Indian grouping (₹1,200; ₹844 crore). Give US dollar figures as published.

76	
77	### Q5 (continued). Dose-response by drug, half-dose and low-dose combinations
78	
79	- D4-01-F26 | Thiazide dose-response (Cochrane) | 60 double-blind placebo trials, 11,282 people, mean 8 weeks, baseline 158/99. Hydrochlorothiazide is dose-related: 6.25 mg 4/2, 12.5 mg 6/3, 25 mg 8/3, 50 mg 11/5 mm Hg. Chlorthalidone 12.5 to 75 mg: 12/4 mm Hg, with no evidence of dose dependence (lowest doses studied lowered BP maximally; low-quality evidence). Thiazides lower systolic more than diastolic (pulse pressure down 4 to 6 vs 3 for ACE inhibitors/ARBs). Potassium falls and uric acid rises with dose; chlorthalidone raised glucose. 90% of trials unclear or high risk of bias. Reading for step 5: chlorthalidone 12.5 is near the top of its BP curve; hydrochlorothiazide 25 (the protocol's substitute) gives about 8 mm Hg alone. Year 2014. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24869750/ | source dated 2014-05 | OPENED | CITED
80	- D4-01-F27 | Quarter doses (meta-analysis) | 42 trials, 20,284 people. A single drug at quarter dose lowered BP 4.7/2.4 mm Hg vs placebo; dual quarter-dose 6.7/4.4; one quadruple quarter-dose trial 22.4/13.1. Against standard-dose monotherapy: single quarter dose +3.7/+2.6 (worse), dual quarter dose +1.3/-0.3 (no different), quadruple -13.1/-7.9 (better). Single and dual quarter-dose therapy had side-effect rates no different from placebo. Mechanism: BP-lowering flattens with dose while dose-related side effects keep rising, so several small doses of different classes beat one big dose. Year 2017. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28584013/ | source dated 2017-07 | OPENED | CITED
81	- D4-01-F28 | TRIUMPH (Sri Lanka, South Asian) | Open-label RCT, 11 urban hospital clinics, 700 patients (mean age 56, 58% women, 29% diabetes, baseline 154/90). Single pill of telmisartan 20 mg + amlodipine 2.5 mg + chlorthalidone 12.5 mg (the protocol's three drugs at low dose) vs usual care. Target BP at 6 months 70% vs 55% (risk difference 12.7%); systolic 9.8 mm Hg lower over follow-up. Dizziness, presyncope or syncope 5.2% vs 2.8%; withdrawals for adverse events 6.6% vs 6.8%. Year 2018. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6583010/ | source dated 2018-08 | OPENED | CITED
82	- D4-01-F29 | GMRx2 trial: triple vs each dual, home BP outcome | Double-blind RCT in Australia, Czech Republic, New Zealand, Poland, Sri Lanka, UK, USA; 1,385 people. Telmisartan 20 + amlodipine 2.5 + indapamide 1.25 vs each dual pair, doses doubled at week 6. Primary outcome home systolic BP at week 12: triple lower by 2.5 vs telmisartan-indapamide, 5.4 vs telmisartan-amlodipine, 4.4 vs amlodipine-indapamide. Clinic control below 140/90: 74% vs 53 to 61%. Adverse-event withdrawals 2% vs 1%. Funded by George Medicines. Year 2024. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39426836/ | source dated 2024-10 | OPENED | CITED
83	- D4-01-F30 | GMRx2 secondary: which dual pair lowers most | 834 randomised to dual pairs. Home systolic at week 12: telmisartan-indapamide 127, telmisartan-amlodipine 130, amlodipine-indapamide 129 mm Hg; TI vs TA -3.1 (CI -4.4 to -1.8). Home control below 130/80: 44%, 39%, 33%. No meaningful differences in kidney function or orthostatic BP. Authors: differences "modest"; "all major dual combinations remain clinically appropriate"; region and ethnicity findings in the parent trial "broadly consistent". Year 2026. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13592818/ | source dated 2026 | OPENED | CITED
84	- D4-01-F31 | QUARTET: quarter-dose quadpill vs standard monotherapy | Double-blind RCT, Australia, 591 adults (12% Asian). Quadpill (irbesartan 37.5, amlodipine 1.25, indapamide 0.625, bisoprolol 2.5) vs irbesartan 150. At 12 weeks systolic 6.9 mm Hg lower (CI 4.9 to 8.9), control 76% vs 58%; at 52 weeks 7.7 mm Hg lower, control 81% vs 62%. Adverse-event withdrawals 4.0% vs 2.4% (p=0.27). Year 2021. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34469767/ | source dated 2021-09 | OPENED | CITED
85	- D4-01-F32 | GENRES rotation (Finland): who responds to amlodipine and thiazide | Placebo-controlled double-blind crossover, 208 Finnish men aged 35 to 60, each took amlodipine 5, bisoprolol 5, hydrochlorothiazide 25 and losartan 50 for 4 weeks each with 4-week placebo gaps. Median 24-hour ambulatory falls: bisoprolol 11/8, losartan 9/6, amlodipine 7/5, hydrochlorothiazide 5/2 mm Hg. Within-person responses correlated most for bisoprolol-losartan and amlodipine-hydrochlorothiazide (the AB/CD split again). Amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide responses rose with age, with placebo BP level and with less night-time dipping; bisoprolol and losartan responses did not vary with any measured trait (age, BMI, skinfold, waist-hip ratio). Men only. Year 2007. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17324745/ | source dated 2007-03 | OPENED | CITED
86	
87	### Q4. Pharmacogenomics: what is known, effect sizes, use in practice
88	
89	- D4-01-F33 | GENRES genome-wide study: weak, unreplicated signals | 228 Finnish men, each on amlodipine, bisoprolol, hydrochlorothiazide and losartan (placebo-controlled crossover); replication in PEAR, GERA I/II, SOPHIA (European ancestry). Only ACY3 variants for bisoprolol reached genome-wide significance, and did not replicate with atenolol. Top 20 variants differed for each drug and none overlapped the 40+ known hypertension genes. Suggestive only: NPHS1 (nephrin) missense rs3814995 for losartan; ALDH1A3 and CLIC5 variants for hydrochlorothiazide. Year 2015. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4330076/ | source dated 2015-01 | OPENED | CITED
90	- D4-01-F34 | Polygenic scores do not predict drug response | In GENRES (about 200 per drug), hypertension polygenic scores (793 top variants or over 1 million variants) showed no significant association with response to amlodipine, bisoprolol, hydrochlorothiazide or losartan after correction; a weak non-significant trend of high score with weaker diuretic response. In Finnish LIFE patients, scores were slightly higher in drug-resistant hypertension (p=0.03, not significant after correction). Year 2020. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7371738/ | source dated 2020-07 | OPENED | CITED
91	- D4-01-F35 | Best single-gene effect sizes are about 3 mm Hg | YEATS4 region (chromosome 12q15, rs7297610), 746 Caucasian and African-American PEAR patients: C/C genotype had 3.4 mm Hg systolic and 2.5 mm Hg diastolic greater response to hydrochlorothiazide than T carriers; no effect with atenolol. NEDD4L (regulates the epithelial sodium channel): GC haplotype associated with greater hydrochlorothiazide response in whites (P=0.0006 systolic), effect size not in abstract. Neither replicated in South Asians (no data found). Years 2013. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3360116/ and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3756535/ | sources dated 2013 | OPENED | CITED
92	- D4-01-F36 | Pharmacogenomics not used in routine hypertension care (2025 review) | Review (Padmanabhan group, Glasgow): clinical translation "remains challenging"; obstacles include "limited clinical actionability, lack of large-scale randomized controlled trials, cost constraints". Polygenic score use for treatment "remains premature". CPIC could not make recommendations even for the GRK4 association; only beta-blocker (metoprolol, CYP2D6) has CPIC/DPWG dosing advice, none for amlodipine, telmisartan or thiazides. Losartan: Swissmedic label notes some patients form under 1% active metabolite instead of about 14% (CYP2C9/CYP3A4 variation). Each common BP variant moves systolic BP by about 1 mm Hg. Year 2025. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12203855/ | source dated 2025 | OPENED | CITED
93	- D4-01-F37 | South Asian pharmacogenomic claims are hypotheses | Same review, in a case scenario: CYP3A5*3 is frequent in South Asians and is "linked with increased plasma amlodipine concentrations"; ACE polymorphism "may explain poor lisinopril response". These are offered as explanations in a teaching case, not shown to change BP response in a trial. Contrast ASCOT (F07): South Asians responded more, not less, to an ACE inhibitor added to amlodipine. Year 2025. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12203855/ | source dated 2025 | OPENED | CITED
94	
95	### Q1 (continued). Sex and body weight
96	
97	- D4-01-F38 | Sex: no difference in outcome benefit by drug class (BPLTTC) | Individual-participant meta-analysis, 51 RCTs, 358,636 people (42% women), median 4.2 years. A 5 mm Hg systolic fall cut major cardiovascular events similarly in women (HR 0.92) and men (0.90), P interaction 1; consistent across age and across drug classes (all P interaction at least 0.14). Authors: "does not substantiate sex-based differences in BP-lowering treatment". Note: this is about event benefit per mm Hg, not about mm Hg per drug. Year 2023. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37485657/ | source dated 2023-07 | OPENED | CITED
98	- D4-01-F39 | Sex and age: amlodipine responds more in women and over 65 | Open-label community trial (ACCT), US, 1,084 patients, amlodipine 5 to 10 mg, 4-week titration then 12 weeks. Mean fall 16.3/12.5 mm Hg; goal response 86% overall, 91.4% women vs 83.0% men (p at or below 0.001), 91.5% at 65 or over vs 84.1% under 65; white 86.0% vs Black 85.9%. The sex difference was not explained by age, weight, mg/kg dose, race, baseline BP or compliance. No placebo arm. Year 1996. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8651122/ | source dated 1996-04-01 | OPENED | CITED
99	- D4-01-F40 | Sex: pharmacokinetics (review table) | 2020 review: amlodipine exposure (AUC, Cmax) higher in women but not after adjusting for weight; telmisartan Cmax higher in women without a BP difference; hydrochlorothiazide no pharmacokinetic sex difference but hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia more frequent in women. Only 43% of ACE inhibitor/ARB trials reported sex-specific data (Rabi 2008, cited there). Plus the amlodipine label (F19): oedema 14.6% women vs 5.6% men. Year 2020. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7218117/ | source dated 2020-04 | OPENED | CITED
100	- D4-01-F41 | Body weight: obese patients respond to both ACE inhibitor and thiazide | TROPHY: 12-week double-blind RCT in 232 obese hypertensives; lisinopril (10 to 40 mg) and hydrochlorothiazide (12.5 to 50 mg) lowered office systolic 9.2 and 10.0 vs 4.6 placebo; diastolic control 60% vs 43% (P<.05) favouring lisinopril. Hydrochlorothiazide raised glucose (+0.31 vs -0.21 mmol/L) and cut potassium by 0.4 mmol/L. Year 1997. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9231834/ | source dated 1997-08 | OPENED | CITED
101	- D4-01-F42 | Body weight: small crossover-free trial and null results | Schmieder 1993: 36 white men, obese (BMI over 27) responded better (diastolic) to metoprolol, lean better to the calcium blocker isradipine (interaction p=0.019); very small. Against this, GENRES (F32) found losartan and bisoprolol response did not vary by BMI, skinfold or waist-hip ratio, and the telmisartan label (F21) says effect is not influenced by weight or BMI. Net: no usable body-weight rule for the protocol drugs. Years 1993, 2007, 2026. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1678609/ | source dated 1993-08 | OPENED | CITED
102	
103	### Q3 (continued). Other guideline rules, and the India programme
104	
105	- D4-01-F43 | WHO 2021: no profile rule for the first drug | WHO recommends drugs from any of three classes as initial treatment: thiazide/thiazide-like, ACE inhibitor/ARB, long-acting dihydropyridine calcium blocker (conditional recommendation); suggests combination therapy, preferably single-pill, as initial treatment. No age or ancestry rule in the text seen. Full guideline and executive summary pages could not be machine-read (Bookshelf verification wall; recommendation tables are images in the PMC summary), so wording is from search results. Year 2021. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8654104/ and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK573629/ | source dated 2021-08 | SNIPPET | SNIPPET
106	- D4-01-F44 | ISH 2020: ancestry rule for Black patients only | Algorithm (as reproduced in secondary sources): step 1 low-dose ACE inhibitor/ARB + dihydropyridine calcium blocker for most; for Black patients step 1 is ARB + calcium blocker or calcium blocker + thiazide-like diuretic; step 2 full doses; step 3 add thiazide-like diuretic. No South Asian-specific rule found in the results. Primary text not opened (publisher page refused). Year 2020. https://karger.com/mpp/article-pdf/30/6/579/3727090/000518812.pdf | source dated 2021 | SNIPPET | SNIPPET
107	- D4-01-F45 | IHCI protocol data: what each step bought (India, 2018 to 2021) | Programme records, 23 districts of Punjab and Maharashtra; 281,209 started on amlodipine 5 mg; 159,292 analysed (36% excluded as not returning in Jan to Mar 2022, 8% off protocol). Clinic BP controlled at step 1 (amlodipine 5 mg): 70% Punjab, 76% Maharashtra. Punjab step 2 = amlodipine 10 mg: cumulative control 75%. Maharashtra step 2 = add telmisartan 40 mg: 76% to 81%. Mean systolic fell 16 mm Hg (from 148) in Punjab and about 15 (from 144) in Maharashtra. Review every 30 days. Limits stated by authors: clinic BP only, no home or ambulatory BP, no data on non-returners, few patients beyond step 2, side effects not recorded. Survivor bias likely inflates control (our reading). Year 2024. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10959138/ | source dated 2024-03-19 | OPENED | CITED
108	- D4-01-F46 | IHCI: why amlodipine starts | All IHCI protocols start amlodipine 5 mg except chronic kidney disease (telmisartan first). Protocols used three drugs: amlodipine, telmisartan (one state enalapril), chlorthalidone or hydrochlorothiazide; procurement at scale within budget was a stated factor. State protocol documents (per search results) say amlodipine needs no metabolic monitoring and can be given to women of childbearing age. The IHCI paper itself gives no physiological "who responds" rationale. The paper was opened; the state-document rationale is from search results only. Year 2024. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10959138/ | source dated 2024-03-19 | OPENED | CITED
109	- D4-01-F47 | Salt sensitivity in India (north-east) | Community study, 374 volunteers (168 hypertensive), 7 days low salt (2.9 g/day) then 7 days high salt (15.2 g/day). Systolic rose 10.7 mm Hg in hypertensives and 9.3 in normotensives on high salt. Salt-sensitive phenotype (mean arterial pressure up 9 mm Hg or more) in 47.6% of hypertensives and 40.8% of normotensives. Extra-salt habit doubled the odds (OR 1.99). Relevance: per F13, salt-sensitive, high-salt patients lose more effect from renin-angiotensin blockers than from calcium blockers. Year 2018. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31044759/ | source dated 2018 | OPENED | CITED
110	- D4-01-F48 | Salt restriction in South Asians lowers BP on top of drugs | RCT, 56 UK Bangladeshi patients with CKD, 6 months: tailored low-salt advice cut urinary sodium from 260 to 103 mmol/day and lowered 24-hour BP by 8/2 mm Hg vs control, independent of medication. Year 2013. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3756453/ | source dated 2013 | OPENED | CITED
111	
112	### Q5 (continued). The protocol's own steps, priced from labels and trials
113	
114	- D4-01-F49 | Telmisartan/amlodipine 4x4 factorial: each protocol step in mm Hg | 8-week double-blind placebo-controlled factorial, 1,461 patients (mean 153/102). Placebo-subtracted seated trough systolic/diastolic: amlodipine 5 mg -12.9/-7.2; amlodipine 10 mg -18.2/-10.9; telmisartan 40 -12.1/-7.2; telmisartan 80 -11.8/-7.8; amlodipine 5 + telmisartan 40 -19.3/-10.3; amlodipine 5 + telmisartan 80 -19.6/-12; amlodipine 10 + telmisartan 40 -22.2/-14; amlodipine 10 + telmisartan 80 -23.9/-13.9. OUR ARITHMETIC along the Gujarat path: step 2 (amlodipine 5 to 10) adds 5.3 systolic; step 3 (add telmisartan 40 to amlodipine 10) adds 4.0; step 4 (telmisartan 40 to 80) adds 1.7. Most of the combination effect was present within 2 weeks. Similar in 65 and over vs under 65, men vs women, diabetes vs not; Black patients "approached" non-Black (237 Black patients). Year 2026 label. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=14f9b590-4c43-439c-a647-9fc2b0fd4d7f | label effective 2026-10-23 | OPENED | CITED
115	- D4-01-F50 | Uncontrolled on amlodipine 10: telmisartan 80 adds nothing over 40 | Double-blind trial, 947 patients not controlled on amlodipine 10 mg, 8 weeks: change -11.1/-9.2 with telmisartan 40 + amlodipine 10, -11.3/-9.3 with telmisartan 80 + amlodipine 10, -7.4/-6.5 staying on amlodipine 10. Difference vs amlodipine 10 alone: -3.7/-2.8 (40 mg) and -3.9/-2.8 (80 mg). So step 4 of the protocol (40 to 80 mg) is worth about 0.2 mm Hg systolic in this trial (OUR ARITHMETIC: 11.3 minus 11.1), while it triggers the lab checks. Year 2026 label. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=14f9b590-4c43-439c-a647-9fc2b0fd4d7f | label effective 2026-10-23 | OPENED | CITED
116	- D4-01-F51 | Uncontrolled on amlodipine 5: adding telmisartan beats going to amlodipine 10, with less oedema | Double-blind trial, 1,097 patients not controlled on amlodipine 5 mg, 8 weeks: telmisartan 40/amlodipine 5 -13.6/-9.4, telmisartan 80/amlodipine 5 -15/-10.6, amlodipine 10 -11.1/-8, amlodipine 5 -6.2/-5.7. Telmisartan 40/amlodipine 5 vs amlodipine 10: -2.4/-1.4 (p<0.05). Oedema events 4.3% on the combinations vs 27.2% on amlodipine 10. Mechanism: the ARB dilates the venous (post-capillary) side as well, so capillary pressure from amlodipine's arteriolar dilation is offset (mechanism from general pharmacology, not stated in the label). Year 2026 label. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=14f9b590-4c43-439c-a647-9fc2b0fd4d7f | label effective 2026-10-23 | OPENED | CITED
117	- D4-01-F52 | ARB dose-response (Cochrane, 9 ARBs) | 46 RCTs, 13,451 people, baseline 156/101. No ARB better than another. 1/8 to 1/4 of the maximum dose gives 60 to 70% of the maximal fall; 1/2 maximum gives 80%; above maximum no further fall. Class trough effect at maximum doses -8/-5 mm Hg (largest trials, publication bias noted); 1 to 12 hours after dose about -12/-7. Year 2008. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6669255/ | source dated 2008-10 | OPENED | CITED
118	
119	- D4-01-F53 | Step 5 analogue: adding a thiazide to amlodipine + ARB | Exforge HCT label: double-blind active-controlled trial, 2,271 patients (mean 170/107, 17% Black). Amlodipine 10 + valsartan 320 + hydrochlorothiazide 25 lowered BP 6.2/3.3 mm Hg more than amlodipine/valsartan, 7.6/5.0 more than valsartan/hydrochlorothiazide, 8.2/5.3 more than amlodipine/hydrochlorothiazide at week 8. "The full blood pressure lowering effect was achieved 2 weeks after being on the maximal dose." Active-controlled, so includes an unknown placebo effect. Valsartan stands in for telmisartan (both ARBs). Year 2026 label. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=18d7820d-471f-4ee2-9ec6-25d8d27c77de | label effective 2026-10-28 | OPENED | CITED
120	- D4-01-F54 | ESH 2023 vs ACC/AHA 2017 (ACC expert summary) | Both: initial therapy from ACE inhibitor, ARB, thiazide/thiazide-like or CCB; ESH also keeps beta-blockers as first-line option. ESH "strongly" favours an initial two-drug combination for most patients, preferred pairs ACE inhibitor/ARB + CCB or + thiazide; ACC/AHA reserves initial two-drug therapy for stage 2, BP over 20/10 above target, and Black patients. Neither summary gives an age-based first-drug rule like NICE; ESH sets age-based targets (under 140/80 at 65 to 79). Year 2024 summary of 2017 and 2023 guidelines. https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/Articles/2024/02/05/11/43/2023-ESH-Hypertension-Guideline-Update | source dated 2024-02-05 | OPENED | CITED
121	- D4-01-F55 | ACC/AHA 2017 Black adults rule | For Black adults with hypertension without heart failure or CKD, including diabetes, initial treatment should include a thiazide-type diuretic or CCB. ESH 2023 (per secondary sources): most Black patients start on a two-drug combination containing a diuretic and a CCB, with each other or with an ACE inhibitor/ARB. Primary guideline texts not opened. Years 2017 and 2023. https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/Articles/2024/02/05/11/43/2023-ESH-Hypertension-Guideline-Update | search result 2026-11-14 | SNIPPET | SNIPPET
122	
123	## NOT FOUND / NOT SEARCHED
124	
125	- NOT FOUND: any crossover or rotation trial (PHYSIC, Cambridge, GENRES type) in Indian or South Asian patients. All personalisation data are Swedish, UK, Finnish or US.
126	- NOT FOUND: a placebo-controlled Indian trial showing that age, sex, renin or salt intake changes response to amlodipine vs telmisartan. Indian drug-vs-drug trials (F11) are small and low quality and show no class differences.
127	- NOT FOUND: plasma renin profile data for Indian hypertensives (only a vitamin D/obesity renin study in an urban Indian sample turned up by title; not opened).
128	- NOT FOUND: drug-level dose-response tables from Wang 2025 Lancet (paywalled); amlodipine 5 vs 10 and telmisartan 40 vs 80 taken from the FDA combination label instead (F49 to F51).
129	- NOT FOUND: a body-weight rule for amlodipine, telmisartan or chlorthalidone backed by a trial; labels and GENRES say response does not vary with BMI for ARBs.
130	- NOT FOUND: any pharmacogenomic test in routine use for amlodipine, telmisartan, losartan or thiazides (CPIC/DPWG guidance exists only for metoprolol); no South Asian replication of YEATS4 or NEDD4L.
131	- NOT SEARCHED (primary text not opened): ISH 2020, ESH 2023, ACC/AHA 2017, WHO 2021 full guideline documents; Indian guidelines (API/CSI) on first drug by profile; IHCI state protocol PDFs (rationale for amlodipine first is SNIPPET only).
132	- NOT SEARCHED: chlorthalidone vs hydrochlorothiazide head-to-head BP trials (Diuretic Comparison Project, outcomes), and chlorthalidone 12.5 vs 25 dose-response trials beyond the Cochrane review.
133	- NOT SEARCHED: losartan in Nigeria or West Africa specifically (CREOLE used perindopril, not losartan).

1	# D4-03 Natural variation and how many readings (agent: claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-14)
2	
3	## Digest
4	
5	1. Error of a home mean (untreated adults): week-to-week SD of mean SBP 6.37 mmHg for 3 days, 4.36 for 7 days (D4-03-F33). 95% band about +/- 8.8 mmHg (3-day) and +/- 6.0 (7-day) (F34, OUR ARITHMETIC).
6	2. Smallest real change at 95%: 8.5 mmHg between two 7-day means, 12.5 between two 3-day means (F34); 13 to 14 between monthly means on stable drugs, where month-to-month SD is 4.7 to 5.1 (F11, F61).
7	3. Single readings in treated older patients: within-week SD 11.8 mmHg (F10, F62).
8	4. 3 days suffice for most; extend to 7 near the threshold (F02, F03, F04). In treated patients a 3-day mean is off the 7-day mean by 3.7 mmHg on average (F06).
9	5. Day 1 runs 2.8/1.4 mmHg high (F01); the effect fades after 6 months of self-monitoring (F16). Sources disagree on discarding it (F17).
10	6. The second reading of a pair averages 2.3 mmHg lower than the first, with wide swings (F36); both predict outcomes equally (F37).
11	7. UK titration trials changed drugs only after "two consecutive months" above target (F13, F56).
12	8. On unchanged drugs, a raised 6-month retest reflects a true rise only 25% of the time (F11); a >10 mmHg clinic rise gave 6 false alarms per true one (F15).
13	9. Only 3% of the apparent spread in individual systolic response to treatment is real (F55).
14	10. Treated Indians (GRAND, Nov 2026): 21.8% masked uncontrolled, 5.1% white-coat uncontrolled (F40). Untreated (India Heart Study): 23.7% white-coat, 18.2% masked (F21).
15	11. India winter minus summer: 9.0/5.6 mmHg in Punjab (F31), 11.1/6.8 in Delhi (F32), both visit readings; Japanese home readings 3 to 4 mmHg (F28).
16	12. Regression to the mean in home BP: a group starting at 156 fell to 143 in a year (F26).
17	
18	Surprises: individual response is nearly all noise (F55); India's seasonal swing is about one drug step (F31, F32); masked uncontrolled is four times white-coat uncontrolled in treated Indians (F40).
19	
20	Against the leads: ESH 2021 says dose self-adjustment is "to be avoided, if not under guidance by the physician in charge" (F07), which fits doctor sign-off. The digital titration trial gained only 3.4 mmHg over usual care (F56).
21	
22	## What this suggests for the product
23	
24	- Suggestion: treat 135/85 as a band, not a line. With 7 valid days, call "still high" without doubt at a mean of about 141 or more. For a mean between 135 and 141, ask for a second cycle before stepping up, as TASMIN-SR and HOME BP did (F13, F34, F56).
25	- Suggestion: if only 3 to 4 days are valid and the mean is within about 9 mmHg of 135, extend measuring rather than decide (F02, F04, F34).
26	- Suggestion: drop day 24 (the first day of the window) when at least 3 other valid days remain, at least in the first 6 months; average both readings of each pair (F01, F16, F36, F37).
27	- Suggestion: never act on one reading except at the 180/110 safety level, and then repeat it after a rest (F53, F54, F62, F13).
28	- Suggestion: report a change as "real" only if two 7-day means differ by 8.5 mmHg or more; label smaller changes "within normal variation" (F34, F61).
29	- Suggestion: add a season flag for India (November to February rise, April to June fall) so winter rises are not over-read and summer lows are checked for over-treatment (F28, F31, F32).
30	- Suggestion: offer home cycles to patients who look controlled in clinic, since about 1 in 5 treated Indians are high only at home (F40).
31	- Suggestion: do not credit or blame the drug on one cycle's change after a high starting value; expect regression to the mean (F26, F55, F57).

1	# D4-05 Biomarkers and adherence signals (agent: claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-14)
2	
3	## Digest
4	
5	The 12 facts that matter most for the biology of the loop:
6	
7	1. By urine or blood drug assay, about 1 in 3 people with apparent resistant hypertension are not taking their drugs (pooled 31.2%, range 3% to 86%) (D4-05-F01); 25% to 42% in UK and Czech LC-MS/MS series (F02, F03).
8	2. In primary care it is far lower: 4.7% of older UK patients (F12). Belgian "resistant" referrals were mostly under-dosed, not non-adherent (F44).
9	3. Odds of non-adherence rise 77% to 85% per added drug (F03; OR 1.57 in Brazil, F07). Each step-up raises the risk.
10	4. Self-report fails: 90.1% adherent by questionnaire vs 32.4% by urine assay (F07). In India, 99DOTS phone self-report had sensitivity 70%, NPV 21% against urine tests (F23).
11	5. Feeding assay results back raised adherence (70% to 92.5%) but did not lower BP in two RCTs (RHYME F05; OUTREACH -5.1 mmHg, NS, F11). Big BP falls come only from uncontrolled before-after data (F04).
12	6. Amlodipine and telmisartan leave no pulse signature (F16, F18); beta-blockers do (F41), diltiazem slightly (F42).
13	7. ARBs raise renin (losartan 2 to 3 times, F19); a 48% fall in aldosterone-to-renin ratio from baseline flagged adherence with 90% sensitivity, 75% specificity (one 40-patient study, F43).
14	8. Chlorthalidone lowers potassium and raises uric acid, dose-related and in step with its BP effect (F21, F22): a weak intake sign.
15	9. Recheck creatinine and potassium 2 to 4 weeks after starting or raising an ARB; continue unless creatinine rises over 30% (KDIGO 2024, F27, F28). eGFR change over 20% (F29) or ACR doubling (F33) is beyond noise.
16	10. HbA1c moves over 2 to 3 months; it cannot judge a 30-day step (F37).
17	11. India's free public list: dipstick at village level; creatinine, urea, uric acid at PHC; potassium and urine ACR sent to a hub; NT-proBNP only at district level (F39).
18	12. Long half-lives blur single assays: amlodipine 30 to 50 h (F17), chlorthalidone 40 to 60 h (F21); a dose just before a test hides gaps (Hawthorne effect, F06).
19	
20	Surprises: cheap reminder devices did nothing in a 53,480-person RCT (F24), but reminder packaging raised pills taken 11% (F46); no Indian drug-assay study for hypertension exists that we found (F15); a smartphone home urine ACR test is FDA-cleared (F49).
21	
22	Against lead 1: non-adherence grows with each added drug (F03), and objective adherence feedback has not yet lowered BP in RCTs (F05, F11).
23	
24	## What this suggests for the product
25	
26	- Suggestion: before any step-up, use signals beyond the patient's word, but do not expect a cheap body signal for the protocol drugs: amlodipine and telmisartan leave no pulse change (F16, F18). Pill counts or photos of the strip and refill dates are the practical first layer (F46, F47, F48).
27	- Suggestion: weight the adherence question by the number of drugs; risk rises about 1.8 times per added drug (F03, F07), so steps 3 to 5 need a stronger check than steps 1 to 2.
28	- Suggestion: borrow the Lane trigger as a rule: if systolic falls less than 10 mmHg after a new drug is added, flag possible non-adherence before the next step (F14).
29	- Suggestion: schedule creatinine and potassium 2 to 4 weeks after telmisartan starts or doubles, with a 30% creatinine-rise rule for doctor review (F27, F28); this fits inside the 30-day cycle.
30	- Suggestion: at chlorthalidone start, a baseline and 2 to 4 week potassium and uric acid gives both a safety check and a weak sign of intake (F21, F22). Potassium needs a hub sample in the public system (F39).
31	- Suggestion: do not use HbA1c or NT-proBNP as step-cycle signals; HbA1c is a 3-monthly check (F37); NT-proBNP is district-level and ₹1,200 to ₹3,520 privately (F35, F36), for suspected heart failure only.
32	- Suggestion: treat a drug assay as a referral-level test, not a loop feature: no Indian assay service or price was found (F15, NOT FOUND below), and RCT benefit on BP is unproven (F05, F11).
33	- Suggestion: if the loop wants an ARB-specific lab sign, a baseline renin or aldosterone-to-renin ratio before telmisartan and a repeat at 2 weeks is the only tested option found (F43); evidence is one 40-patient study.

Diuresis starts about 2.6 hours after a dose and lasts up to 72 hours; mean half-life 40 hours (53 hours after 50 mg, 60 hours after 100 mg); binds red-cell carbonic anhydrase. Mechanism (textbook physiology, not stated in the label): blocking the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal tubule delivers more sodium to the collecting duct, where it is swapped for potassium; less volume raises urate reabsorption. So a modest potassium fall and uric acid rise are expected chemical signs of taking it. Label also lists hyperglycemia and hypomagnesaemia. Year 2026. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=36ef8d83-45f2-4873-b7cb-1be096d14d18 | source dated 2026-10 | OPENED | CITED
64	
65	- D4-05-F22 | Thiazide potency: potassium and urate fall and rise in step with BP effect | Meta-analysis of 30 placebo-controlled dose-ranging trials (4,683 people; 26 HCTZ, 3 chlorthalidone, 1 bendroflumethiazide): dose to lower systolic BP by 10 mmHg was 8.6 mg chlorthalidone vs 26.4 mg hydrochlorothiazide; the potency order for serum potassium and urate matched the order for BP. So at protocol doses (chlorthalidone 12.5 mg, HCTZ 25 mg) a potassium fall and urate rise go with the drug's BP effect; their absence is weak evidence it is not being taken. Western trials. Year 2012. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/22547443 | source dated 2012 | OPENED (abstract) | CITED

69	- D4-05-F23 | India, 99DOTS phone-call adherence vs urine isoniazid test | 597 Indian TB patients; urine isoniazid tests on unannounced home visits. Adherence by urine 88%. 99DOTS (patient-reported calls) sensitivity 70%, specificity 61%, PPV 93%, NPV 21%, accuracy 69%. Adding health-worker-entered doses raised sensitivity to 85% but cut specificity to 39%. Authors: health workers must contact about 10 patients flagged non-adherent by 99DOTS to find 2 who truly are not taking drugs. Indian evidence that a phone self-report signal misclassifies about 1 in 3. Year 2020. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/32221550 | source dated 2020 | OPENED (full text) | CITED

Null. Year 2017. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/28241271 | source dated 2017 | OPENED (abstract) | CITED

Treatment success OR 1.14 (0.99 to 1.30) in RCTs, very low certainty; more adverse events reported (OR 1.57). Year 2025. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41087928 | source dated 2025 | OPENED (abstract) | CITED

Initial GFR estimate uses serum creatinine plus an equation (eGFRcr); add cystatin C (eGFRcr-cys) when creatinine is less accurate (muscle mass, diet, some drugs) and the decision depends on GFR. "Interpretation of SCr level requires consideration of dietary intake." Year 2024. https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/KDIGO-2024-CKD-Guideline.pdf | source dated 2024-03 | OPENED | CITED

Year 2024. https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/KDIGO-2024-CKD-Guideline.pdf | source dated 2024-03 | OPENED | CITED

Practice Point 2.1.4: after starting haemodynamically active therapy, eGFR falls of more than 30% exceed expected variability. The text says acute creatinine rises (eGFR falls) under 20% to 30% "are expected and do not warrant changes", because ACEi/ARBs lower BP and alter arteriolar flow (standard physiology, not KDIGO's words: the efferent arteriole relaxes, glomerular pressure falls, filtration falls a little; a haemodynamic, reversible effect). Algorithm: if more than 30% fall, review drugs (diuretics, NSAIDs), volume depletion, consider renal artery stenosis. Year 2024. https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/KDIGO-2024-CKD-Guideline.pdf | source dated 2024-03 | OPENED | CITED

Fingerprick microsampling noted as enabling point-of-care testing. Year 2024. https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/KDIGO-2024-CKD-Guideline.pdf | source dated 2024-03 | OPENED | CITED

Telmisartan label: hyperkalaemia risk mainly with advanced kidney disease, heart failure, potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics or potassium-containing salt substitutes; "Consider periodic determinations of serum electrolytes". Year 2024 and 2012. https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/KDIGO-2024-CKD-Guideline.pdf | source dated 2024-03 | OPENED | CITED

Albuminuria marks damage to the glomerular filter and endothelium and predicts kidney and cardiovascular events independently of eGFR. Year 2024. https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/KDIGO-2024-CKD-Guideline.pdf | source dated 2024-03 | OPENED | CITED

Confirm a strip-positive result with a lab ACR; confirm a random ACR of 30 mg/g or more with a first morning sample. Practice Point 2.1.5: a doubling of ACR on a later test exceeds lab variability; smaller swings may be noise. Year 2024. https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/KDIGO-2024-CKD-Guideline.pdf | source dated 2024-03 | OPENED | CITED

Thresholds summarised from ESC and the ICON-RELOADED study: non-acute rule-out NT-proBNP under 125 pg/mL (BNP under 35 pg/mL); acute rule-out under 300 pg/mL (BNP under 100); acute rule-in by age 450 (under 50 years), 900 (50 to 75), 1,800 pg/mL (over 75). Higher with age, female sex, kidney disease and atrial fibrillation; lower with obesity. Secondary review, not the ESC text itself. Year 2026. https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13513204 | source dated 2026 | OPENED (full text) | CITED

Misleading in anaemias and other conditions that change red-cell turnover, some haemoglobin variants, sickle cell disease (HbSS: cannot be measured), pregnancy and kidney failure. Point-of-care A1C "can offer timely opportunities for treatment adjustments" but may be less accurate than lab assays. Relevance: thiazide-type diuretics can raise glucose (chlorthalidone label lists hyperglycaemia), so HbA1c is a slow, months-scale check, not a step-cycle signal. Year 2026. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12690178/ | source dated 2026-01 | OPENED | CITED

# D3-01 Claims check: D1-01 and D1-02 clinical evidence (agent: Claude Sonnet 5.5, 2026-11-13)

## Verdict

Checked 53 fact IDs against the source (abstracts via NCBI E-utilities; PHTI PDFs; ResMed, AAFA, GOV.UK, SEC, ClinicalTrials.gov, trade pages). Status: CONFIRMED 48, CORRECTED 5, CONTESTED 0, NOT FOUND 0. Every number in the two notes matched its source. The corrections are precision fixes (a comparator, a date, a funder, a denominator), and five wordings in the Decision brief or DT1 need changing (listed under "Sentences to change"). Four SNIPPET facts were upgraded to OPENED: Propeller ceased operations, Teva Digihaler withdrawal, Rejoyn primary result, CRHCP incentives and free drugs.

Sentences to change in the Decision brief:
1. Tucker 6.1 mmHg: "with intensive co-interventions (titration by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling)", not "including dose changes".
2. STRONG-HF 15.2% vs 23.3%: adjusted, down-weighted Kaplan-Meier estimates at 180 days; high-intensity arm had four clinic visits and more adverse events (41% vs 29%).
3. "Telemonitoring without a therapy change" (TELE-HF, BEAT-HF): the abstracts do not show that. BEAT-HF had nurse "protocolized actions". Say "telemonitoring without a mandated dose protocol".
4. 3.3% at day 30: the median of 93 popular Android mental-health apps (2019), not "3.3% of users".
5. Rural China: add that the programme also gave discounted or free drugs and paid village doctors incentive supplements tied to control rates (now OPENED).

## Never say
- "Self-monitoring plus dose changes cut BP by 6.1 mmHg" (6.1 is any intensive co-intervention).
- "15.2% of patients against 23.3%" for STRONG-HF as if raw counts (raw: 74/506 and 109/502).
- "25% of Trivandrum heart-failure patients" (it is 25% of the 62% with reduced ejection fraction).
- "COBRA-BPS health workers changed doses" (they monitored and counselled; trained physicians treated).
- "Both heart-failure telemonitoring trials had no therapy change" (BEAT-HF protocolised actions).
- "Adherence rose from 30% to 84%" (two arms, not before and after).
- "3.3% of mental-health app users stay to day 30" (median app).
- "The China result is the protocol alone" (free or discounted drugs and incentives included).
- "Warfarin self-dosing beats self-testing" as a head-to-head result (separate trial sets, indirect).
- "Propeller shut down in <date>" (no date on the ResMed page); "ResMed closed Propeller purchase 31 Jan 2019" (press release is 7 Jan 2019).
- "PHTI says digital diabetes tools fail" without "non-continuous glucose monitor, type 2, US".

## Checks
| Fact ID | Claim as noted | Status | Verified value, source, date opened |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1-01-F01 | TASMINH2: 527 pts, 3.7 mmHg at 6 mo, 5.4 (2.4 to 8.5) at 12 mo; leg swelling 32% vs 22% | CONFIRMED | Primary is systolic change at 6 and 12 months, 1:1 vs usual care, 91% analysed, no imputation; funder UK Dept of Health programmes. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20619448/ (efetch, 13 Nov 2026). Patients had to be "willing to self-manage". |
----
46:- D3-04-F09 GRAND study, 18 centres in 12 states, 1,920 treated hypertensive patients aged 20-70 (all on drugs 3+ months and regular clinic attenders), 7 days home BP. Controlled by clinic BP alone 77.7%; by clinic plus home BP 55.9%; masked uncontrolled 21.8%; white-coat 5.1%; sustained uncontrolled 17.2%. Published 2026-11-06. PMID 42995223; https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42995223 OPENED.

Blood pressure control assessed by clinic and home blood pressure measurements 
among hypertensive patients in India: results from the GRAND study.

Hypertension is a prevalent non-communicable disease and a significant 
cardiovascular risk factor in India, affecting 25% of adults. Among those 
treated, only 52.5% achieved controlled clinic blood pressure (CBP). We 
investigated blood pressure (BP) control in India using CBP and home BP (HBP). 
This multicenter, cross-sectional study across 18 centers in 12 states within 7 
regions enrolled hypertensive participants aged 20-70 years receiving 
antihypertensive medications for ≥3 months who regularly visited their clinic. A 
background survey and four CBP readings were collected at baseline ("Clinic 
Visit 1") and Clinic Visit 2. Participants underwent HBP monitoring for seven 
days. Based on average CBP across the two clinic visits and average HBP, 
participants were classified as having well-controlled hypertension 
(CBP < 140/90 mmHg and HBP < 135/85 mmHg), white-coat uncontrolled hypertension 
(WUCH; CBP ≥ 140/90 mmHg and HBP < 135/85 mmHg), masked uncontrolled 
hypertension (MUCH; CBP < 140/90 mmHg and HBP ≥ 135/85 mmHg), or sustained 
uncontrolled hypertension (SUCH; CBP ≥ 140/90 mmHg and HBP ≥ 135/85 mmHg). Among 
1920 participants, 1578 with appropriate CBP and HBP readings were analyzed. Of 
these, 55.9% had well-controlled hypertension, 5.1% had WUCH, 21.8% had MUCH, 
and 17.2% had SUCH. The proportion classified as controlled was 77.7% using 
clinic BP alone versus 55.9% using both clinic and home BP, a difference of 21.8 
percentage points. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating HBP 
alongside CBP for comprehensive assessment of BP control and identification of 
BP control phenotypes. Clinical trial registration: Registered at Clinical 
Trials Registry-India (CTRI) under CTRI/2023/02/049486 on 06 February 2023.

Comment in
    J Clin Hypertens (Greenwich). 2024 May;26(5):594. doi: 10.1111/jch.14815.

One-fourth of death in India is attributed to cardiovascular disease (CVD) and 
more than 80% is related to ischemic heart disease and stroke. The main risk 
factor for CVD is hypertension. Every third person in India suffers from 
hypertension and the prevalence increased drastically in the past 20 years, 
especially among the youngest age group of 20 and 44 years. Regardless of being 
under anti-hypertension medication, the blood pressure (BP) control rate in the 
country is still low ranging between 6% and 28% only. Assessing the "true BP 
control rate" should be performed using both clinic BP measurement and 
out-of-office BP measurement as the latter shows better prognosis for patients' 
hypertension and CVD outcomes. Home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) shows 
superiority over ambulatory BP measurement as multiple measurements can be 
collected at the patient's convenience. Only limited evidence on HBPM in India 
is available and it's either lacking in hypertension participants or of a small 
sample size. This study will investigate the real BP control status among 2000 
hypertensive patients from 18 centers in 12 states across Pan-India. The outcome 
of this study will emphasize the value of establishing BP control management 
practice guidelines suitable for physicians and help policymakers in building 
proper strategies for hypertension management to reduce the CVD burden on the 
health situation in India.

among hypertensive patients in India: results from the GRAND Study.

Home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) is recommended for the management of 
hypertension; however, patients' understanding of hypertension and HBPM remains 
insufficient. This multicenter cross-sectional study assessed knowledge of 
hypertension and HBPM among 1920 patients receiving pharmacological treatment 
across 12 states in India and identified factors associated with relatively 
higher knowledge. Knowledge was evaluated across four domains: understanding of 
clinic and home blood pressure (BP) thresholds, awareness of causes of 
hypertension, recognition of risks associated with uncontrolled BP, and 
awareness of the benefits of HBPM. The median knowledge score was 1 (range 0-7), 
indicating generally low knowledge. Knowledge varied across domains, with 
particularly poor understanding of BP thresholds and limited awareness of HBPM 
benefits, while awareness of causes and complications was relatively higher but 
still insufficient. Relatively higher knowledge (≥75th percentile) was observed 
in 38.0% of participants and was more common among participants with prior HBPM 
experience than among those without prior HBPM experience (46.9% vs. 29.9%, 
p < 0.001). Higher education, type of healthcare facility, and prior HBPM 
experience were associated with relatively higher knowledge. These findings 
suggest that knowledge of hypertension among patients in India is limited and 
domain-specific, with critical gaps in areas essential for interpreting and 
utilizing BP measurements. Improving hypertension management may require not 
only promoting HBPM but also strengthening patient education. Clinical trial 
registration status: Registered at Clinical Trials Registry-India (CTRI) under 
CTRI/2023/02/049486 on 06 February 2023.

342	corresponding to systolic blood pressure-lowering efficacy of <10 mm Hg, 10-19 
343	mm Hg, and ≥20 mm Hg, respectively, from a baseline of 154 mm Hg. A model was 
344	developed to calculate efficacy for any combination of antihypertensives and

347	Systematic Review and Meta-analysis Protocols (INPLASY202410036).

689	BACKGROUND: Salt sensitivity is known to increase the risk of cardiovascular 
690	diseases in both normotensive and hypertensive subjects. The population in the 
691	northeastern region of India consumes excess dietary salt but their 
692	saltsensitive phenotype is not known.
693	METHODS: We did a community-based exploratory study using volunteers in the 
694	northeastern region of India to determine salt-sensitive (SS) and salt-resistant 
695	(SR) phenotypes. A total of 374 (206 normotensive and 168 hypertensive) subjects 
696	who gave informed consent were stabilized for salt with 7 days of a low-salt 
697	(2.9 g/day) diet followed by 7 days of a high-salt (15.2 g/day) diet. SS was 
698	defined as an increase of mean arterial blood pressure ≥9 mmHg after a high-salt 
699	diet.

701	normotensive subjects and 10.7 mmHg in hypertensive subjects, with a modest 
702	effect on diastolic blood pressure (6.9 mmHg in normotensive and 8.2 mmHg in 
703	hypertensive subjects) after a high-salt diet. Salt-sensitive phenotype was 
704	present in 40.8% of normotensive and 47.6% of hypertensive subjects. Resistance 
705	to introduction of high salt was observed in 43.7% of normotensive and 33.9% of 
706	hypertensive subjects. Consumption of extra salt (adjusted OR 1.99, 95% CI 
707	1.25-3.18) was independently associated with salt sensitivity.
708	CONCLUSION: Salt sensitivity was found in a large proportion of normotensive and 
709	hypertensive subjects. Restriction of salt intake could be an effective 
710	intervention to control hypertension among salt-sensitive subjects.

3	Home blood pressure monitoring schedule: optimal and minimum based on 2122 
4	individual participants' data.
5	
6	OBJECTIVES: Home blood pressure (HBP) monitoring has become a primary method for 
7	hypertension diagnosis and management. This analysis aimed to investigate the 
8	optimal and minimum schedule for HBP monitoring.
9	METHODS: A retrospective analysis of cross-sectional data was performed, which 
10	involved HBP and 24-h ambulatory blood pressure (ABP) monitoring in adults 
11	performed within the context of clinical studies in Finland, Greece and UK. 
12	Participants with six to seven HBP monitoring days and at least 12 HBP readings 
13	were included. The stability of HBP was assessed by evaluating the average value 
14	of an increasing number of readings and its variability (SD). Its association 
15	with awake ABP was also assessed.
16	RESULTS: Data from 2122 participants were analysed (mean age 53.9 ± 11.3 years, 
17	males 53%, treated 34%). A progressive HBP decline was observed in succeeding 
18	days, reaching a plateau after day 3. Day 1 HBP was higher than in the next days 
19	by about 2.8/1.4 mmHg (systolic/diastolic, P < 0.001). In a 3-day HBP monitoring 
20	schedule, the exclusion of day 1 reduced average HBP and SD, with a clinically 
21	important HBP decline in 115 participants (5%) and different hypertension 
22	diagnosis in 120 participants (6%). For schedules including more than three HBP 
23	monitoring days, the exclusion of day 1 had negligible impact. The 3-day average 
24	HBP was strongly correlated with awake ABP, with a little improvement 
25	thereafter.
26	CONCLUSION: These data support the recommendation for 7 days of HBP monitoring 
27	with a minimum of 3 days. Readings of the first day should be discarded, 
28	particularly when the minimum 3-day monitoring schedule is obtained (average 
29	readings of second and third day).

43	BACKGROUND: Self-monitoring of blood pressure better predicts prognosis than 
44	clinic measurement, is popular with patients, and endorsed in hypertension 
45	guidelines. However, there is uncertainty over the optimal self-monitoring 
46	schedule. We therefore aimed to determine the optimum schedule to predict future 
47	cardiovascular events and determine "true" underlying blood pressure.
48	METHODS: Six electronic databases were searched from November 2009 (updating a 
49	National Institute for Health and Care Excellence [NICE] systematic review) to 
50	April 2017. Studies that compared aspects of self-monitoring schedules to either 
51	prognosis or reliability/reproducibility in hypertensive adults were included. 
52	Data on study and population characteristics, self-monitoring regime, and 
53	outcomes were extracted by 2 reviewers independently.
54	RESULTS: From 5,164 unique articles identified, 25 met the inclusion criteria. 
55	Twelve studies were included from the original NICE review, making a total of 37 
56	studies. Increasing the number of days of measurement improved prognostic power: 
57	72%-91% of the theoretical maximum predictive value (asymptotic maximum hazard 
58	ratio) was reached by 3 days and 86%-96% by 7 days. Increasing beyond 3 days of 
59	measurement did not result in better correlation with ambulatory monitoring. 
60	There was no convincing evidence that the timing or number of readings per day 
61	had an effect, or that ignoring the first day's measurement was necessary.
62	CONCLUSIONS: Home blood pressure should be measured for 3 days, increased to 7 
63	only when mean blood pressure is close to a diagnostic or treatment threshold. 
64	Other aspects of a monitoring schedule can be flexible to facilitate patient 
65	uptake of and adherence with self-monitoring.

77	Pressure: Results From the Improving the Detection of Hypertension Study.
78	
79	Background Obtaining out-of-clinic blood pressure ( BP ) measurements to confirm 
80	a diagnosis of hypertension is recommended before initiating treatment. There 
81	are few empiric data available on the number of measurements required to 
82	reliably estimate BP on home BP monitoring ( HBPM ). Methods and Results We 
83	analyzed data from 316 community-dwelling adults not taking antihypertensive 
84	medication from the IDH (Improving the Detection of Hypertension) study who 
85	performed HBPM for 14 days. The reliability of home BP measurements was assessed 
86	using the intraclass correlation coefficient and as the percentage of 
87	participants with an absolute difference in home BP <10 mm Hg between weeks. The 
88	reliability of home hypertension status was assessed by the κ statistic. In the 
89	IDH study, 13.6% of participants had clinic hypertension and 18.0% had home 
90	hypertension. Mean home systolic and diastolic BP exhibited excellent 
91	reliability and sufficient agreement using the average of 2 morning and 2 
92	evening BP readings for a minimum of 2 days of HBPM and a single morning and 
93	single evening or 2 morning BP readings for a minimum of 3 days. For diagnosing 
94	home hypertension, there was good agreement with a minimum of 3 days of HBPM 
95	using the average of 2 morning and 2 evening measurements or a single morning 
96	and single evening BP reading. A greater number of days was required for the 
97	other HBPM strategies. Conclusions Using the average of morning and evening 
98	readings, 3 days of HBPM are needed to reliably estimate mean home BP and 
99	diagnose out-of-clinic hypertension.
