111	BACKGROUND: Home blood pressure (BP) monitoring over a 7-day period is 
112	recommended to confirm the diagnosis of hypertension.
113	METHODS: We determined upper and lower home BP thresholds with >90% positive 
114	predictive value and >90% negative predictive value using 1 to 6 days of 
115	monitoring to identify high home BP (systolic BP ≥130 mm Hg or diastolic BP ≥80 
116	mm Hg) based on 7 days of home BP monitoring. The sample included 361 adults 
117	from the Improving the Detection of Hypertension Study who were not taking 
118	antihypertensive medication. We used two 7-day periods, at least 3 days apart, 
119	the first being a sampling period and the second a reference period. For each 
120	number of days in the sampling period, we determined the percentage of 
121	participants who had a high likelihood of having (>90% positive predictive 
122	value) or not having (>90% negative predictive value) high BP and would not need 
123	to continue home BP monitoring. Only the participants in an uncertain category 
124	(ie, positive predictive value ≤90% and negative predictive value ≤90%) after 
125	each day were carried forward to the next day of home BP monitoring.

127	women), 38.0% had high home BP during the reference period. There were 63.7%, 
128	17.1%, 10.5%, 3.3%, 3.6%, and 1.4% participants who would not need to continue 
129	after 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 days of monitoring.
130	CONCLUSIONS: In most people, high home BP can be identified or excluded with a 
131	high degree of confidence with 3 days or less of monitoring.

141	analysis of data from two randomized controlled trials.

143	BACKGROUND: Little evidence exists around the optimal frequency of 
144	self-monitoring of blood pressure (BP). Testing too frequently can lead to 
145	erroneous management changes due to random "noise" leading to raised 
146	measurements by chance. This study used recent trial data to evaluate 
147	self-monitored BP over time, aiming to determine how frequently patients should 
148	self-monitor.
149	METHODS: Data from patients with home BP ≤135/85 mmHg on stable medication in 
150	the self-monitoring groups of two trials were analysed using a mixed effects 
151	model. The primary outcome was mean change in BP per month. Secondary outcomes 
152	included intra-individual BP variability, and probability of truly raised BP 
153	over time.
154	RESULTS: 232 participants from HOMEBP, and 582 participants from TASMINH4 were 
155	included. The mean changes in systolic BP per month per study were -0.1 mmHg 
156	[standard deviation (SD) 0.6 mmHg], and -0.2mmHg [SD 0.7 mmHg], respectively. 
157	Intra-individual systolic variability (SD) per month was 4.7 and 5.1 mmHg 
158	respectively. Using TASMINH4 data, from a starting systolic BP of 130 mmHg, 
159	re-testing BP after 6 months resulted in a probability of 18% that BP ≥135 mmHg, 
160	with a 25% probability that this reflected truly raised BP; after 12 months the 
161	probability of a raised reading was 26% with a 65% probability this reflected a 
162	true rise.
163	CONCLUSIONS: In the absence of medication changes, there was very little change 
164	in mean self-monitored BP per month, with larger variability within an 
165	individual's monthly submitted readings. For people with initially controlled BP 
166	and stable medication, repeating self-monitoring at 12 months is likely to be 
167	appropriate in guiding management.

There have now been several large trials into self-monitoring of blood pressure, where participants on treatment for hypertension submit frequent home BP readings for at least a year [ 2 ]. These trials provide an opportunity to examine changes in self-monitored BP over time, including variability within reported monthly readings and month by month trends, both for individuals and across study populations. The aim of this study was to determine how frequently patients with controlled treated hypertension should self-monitor to maintain blood pressure to reduce the risk of misclassification of BP as being above threshold. METHODS Data sources Data from the self-monitoring arms of the HOMEBP and TASMINH4 trials were examined [ 13 , 14 ]. HOMEBP [ 13 ] was a randomized controlled trial evaluating a digital intervention which involved self-monitoring of blood pressure. It included 622 participants with hypertension, recruited from 76 general practices, allocated to either self-monitoring with a digital intervention (305 participants) or usual care groups (317 participants). Each month participants in the self-monitoring arm submitted seven consecutive days of home BP readings. If mean home BP was controlled for three consecutive months (defined as 100–134/≤84 mmHg diastolic), patients reduced self-monitoring frequency to once every 8 weeks, but with monitoring reverting back to monthly if mean blood pressure subsequently rose ≥135/85 mmHg. Data were available from 271 participants in the self-monitoring arm over one year, which were considered for this analysis. In TASMINH4 [ 14 ] patients with hypertension (BP >140/90mmHg) were randomized to usual care (394 participants), self-monitoring alone (391 participants) or self-monitoring with telemonitoring (389 participants). For those undertaking self-monitoring only, they were provided with a colour chart to help understand their BP readings, and guide them regarding appropriate management. Participants in the telemonitoring group sent readings via SMS, which used the same algorithm as the colour chart to alert patients to contact their surgery if required, as well as presenting readings to clinicians via a web interface. The self-monitoring groups measured their blood pressure twice daily for the first seven days of every month over a 12-month period. 12-month follow-up data were available for 655 participants. Included populations The following additional inclusion criteria were applied to both HOMEBP and TASMNH4 self-monitoring datasets: participants had to have been on a stable dose of their antihypertensive medication for at least 4 weeks, with no clinical indication for adjustment to their medication at their baseline study visit. They had to have submitted more than one month of BP readings during either trial. Any BP readings submitted after a change in medication were removed from the analysis. Outcomes The primary outcome was overall mean change in systolic BP (SBP) and diastolic BP (DBP) per month for each of the included populations. The secondary outcomes were the probability of an individual's BP rising to above threshold at increasing timepoints, the proportions of these readings reflecting true or false positive results, and the variability of systolic and diastolic BP measurements within a set of submitted results per participant. Analysis A mixed effects regression on SBP was performed, using time coefficients to quantify the change in SBP per calendar month. These time coefficients were treated as person-level random effects, so that the mean time coefficient quantified the mean change per month, and the random effects standard deviation (SD) quantified the between-person variation in change per month. The residual SD from the model was interpreted as an estimate of short-term intra-participant BP variability. These regression results were used to estimate probabilities of SBP being above contemporary UK treatments threshold (≥135 mmHg) [ 15 ] at subsequent re-measurement; in particular, the residual SD was incorporated to distinguish the probabilities of “true positives” (observed and true SBP≥135 mmHg) and “false positives” (observed SBP≥135 mmHg, but true SBP < 135 mmHg). DBP was analysed similarly (except for the threshold for hypertension being ≥85mmHg). Fitted values and residuals were then calculated for both SBP and DBP models, including the correlations between them, in order to define a bivariate model of BP progression [ 9 , 11 ]. From this, we calculated probabilities of either the SBP being truly above threshold, the DBP being truly above threshold, or both. Any of these three possibilities were defined as hypertension. Analyses were initially performed on data collected for HOMEBP and then repeated on data from TASMINH4. For the secondary outcome of probability of an individual's BP rising to above threshold at increasing timepoints, modelling was performed using TASMINH4, as it was the larger dataset. Stata 18.0 (StataCorp, 2023) was used for all analyses. 10	blood pressure (BP) control that puts patients with hypertension at elevated 
11	cardiovascular risk. Studies of medication adherence for apparent 
12	treatment-resistant hypertension (aTRH) vary significantly with respect to 
13	design, methods, and setting, and, as a result, have produced highly variable 
14	figures describing the prevalence of nonadherence. This review aimed to describe 
15	the prevalence and potential moderators of medication nonadherence estimates for

19	measured medication adherence for patients with uncontrolled BP despite being 
20	prescribed three or more antihypertensive medications of different classes. By 
21	using a random effects model, the pooled prevalence of nonadherence was 31.2% 
22	(95% confidence interval = 20.2-44.7, I = 99.50) with nonadherence rates ranging

25	measures of adherence and/or pharmacy data reported lower levels of nonadherence 
26	than studies using more objective methods, such as liquid chromatography-mass 
27	spectrometry in single time-point bioassays or directly observed therapy.

29	problem among aTRH patients. Identifying the most accurate and clinically

403	Nonadherence to antihypertensive medication is common, especially in those with 
404	apparent treatment-resistant hypertension (true treatment-resistant hypertension 
405	requires exclusion of nonadherence), and its routine detection is supported by 
406	clinical guidelines. Chemical adherence testing is a reliable and valid method 
407	to detect adherence, yet methods are unstandardized and are not ubiquitous. This 
408	article describes the principles of chemical adherence testing for hypertensive 
409	patients and provides a set of recommendations for centers wishing to develop 
410	the test. We recommend testing should be done in either of two instances: (1) in 
411	those who have resistant hypertension or (2) in those on 2 antihypertensives who 
412	have a less than 10 mm Hg drop in systolic blood pressure on addition of the 
413	second antihypertensive medication. Furthermore, we recommend that verbal 
414	consent is secured before undertaking the test, and the results should be 
415	discussed with the patient. Based on medications prescribed in United Kingdom, 
416	European Union, and United States, we list top 20 to 24 drugs that cover >95% of 
417	hypertension prescriptions which may be included in the testing panel. 
418	Information required to identify these medications on mass spectrometry 
419	platforms is likewise provided. We discuss issues related to ethics, sample 
420	collection, transport, stability, urine versus blood samples, qualitative versus 
421	quantitative testing, pharmacokinetics, instrumentation, validation, quality 
422	assurance, and gaps in knowledge. We consider how to best present, interpret, 
423	and discuss chemical adherence test results with the patient. In summary, this 
424	guidance should help clinicians and their laboratories in the development of 
425	chemical adherence testing of prescribed antihypertensive drugs.

492	IMPORTANCE: Forgetfulness is a major contributor to nonadherence to chronic 
493	disease medications and could be addressed with medication reminder devices.
494	OBJECTIVE: To compare the effect of 3 low-cost reminder devices on medication 
495	adherence.
496	DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This 4-arm, block-randomized clinical trial 
497	involved 53 480 enrollees of CVS Caremark, a pharmacy benefit manager, across 
498	the United States. Eligible participants were aged 18 to 64 years and taking 1 
499	to 3 oral medications for long-term use. Participants had to be suboptimally 
500	adherent to all of their prescribed therapies (with a medication possession 
501	ratio of 30% to 80%) in the 12 months before randomization. Participants were 
502	stratified on the basis of the medications they were using at randomization: 
503	medications for cardiovascular or other nondepression chronic conditions (the 
504	chronic disease stratum) and antidepressants (the antidepressant stratum). In 
505	each stratum, randomization occurred within blocks defined by whether all of the 
506	patient's targeted medications were dosed once daily. Patients were randomized 
507	to receive in the mail a pill bottle strip with toggles, digital timer cap, or 
508	standard pillbox. The control group received neither notification nor a device. 
509	Data were collected from February 12, 2013, through March 21, 2015, and data 
510	analyses were on the intention-to-treat population.
511	MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was optimal adherence 
512	(medication possession ratio ≥80%) to all eligible medications among patients in 
513	the chronic disease stratum during 12 months of follow-up, ascertained using 
514	pharmacy claims data. Secondary outcomes included optimal adherence to 
515	cardiovascular medications among patients in the chronic disease stratum as well 
516	as optimal adherence to antidepressants.
517	RESULTS: Of the 53 480 participants, mean (SD) age was 45 (12) years and 56% 
518	were female. In the primary analysis, 15.5% of patients in the chronic disease 
519	stratum assigned to the standard pillbox, 15.1% assigned to the digital timer 
520	cap, 16.3% assigned to the pill bottle strip with toggles, and 15.1% assigned to 
521	the control arm were optimally adherent to their prescribed treatments during 
522	follow-up. There was no statistically significant difference in the odds of 
523	optimal adherence between the control and any of the devices (standard pillbox: 
524	odds ratio [OR], 1.03 [95% CI, 0.95-1.13]; digital timer cap: OR, 1.00 [95% CI, 
525	0.92-1.09]; and pill bottle strip with toggles: OR, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.85-1.04]). 
526	In direct comparisons, the odds of optimal adherence were higher with a standard 
527	pillbox than with the pill bottle strip (OR, 1.10 [95% CI, 1.00-1.21]). 
528	Secondary analyses yielded similar results.
529	CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Low-cost reminder devices did not improve adherence 
530	among nonadherent patients who were taking up to 3 medications to treat common 
531	chronic conditions. The devices may have been more effective if coupled with 
532	interventions to ensure consistent use or if targeted to individuals with an 
533	even higher risk of nonadherence.

566	bendroflumethiazide. Studies included a total of 4683 subjects in >53 comparison 
567	arms. Meta-regression of the effect of thiazides on systolic BP showed a

575	different potency. This may account for differences in the antihypertensive

701	relative change in ARR before and after treatment initiation, provided high 
702	accuracy for determination of therapeutic compliance, with an AUC of 0.900 at 
703	2 weeks and 0.886 at 8 weeks. A cut-off of -48% of ΔARR provided 90% sensitivity 
704	and 75% specificity, at 2 and 8 weeks. In conclusion, the measurement of ΔARR is 
705	a powerful test, cheap and widely available to accurately identify the 
706	non-adherence to RAAS inhibitors treatment. Herein we propose the implementation 
707	of ΔARR in clinical practice through a multi-step flow-chart for the management 
708	of patients with uncontrolled blood pressure, with identification of those

770	year of first recruitment, country, and health outcomes attributable to 
771	antihypertensive medication nonadherence were extracted. Two reviewers screened 
772	abstracts and full texts, classified countries according to levels of income and 
773	locations, and extracted data. The Joanna Briggs Institute prevalence critical 
774	appraisal tool was used to rate the included studies. Prevalence meta-analyses 
775	were conducted using a fixed-effects model, and trends in prevalence were 
776	analyzed using meta-regression. The certainty of evidence concerning the effect 
777	of health consequences of nonadherence was rated according to Grading of 
778	Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations. A total of 161 studies

Meaning There is heterogeneity in blood pressure response to drug therapy for hypertension, of a magnitude that warrants further research. Importance Hypertension is the leading risk factor for premature death worldwide. Multiple blood pressure–lowering therapies are available but the potential for maximizing benefit by personalized targeting of drug classes is unknown. Objective To investigate and quantify the potential for targeting specific drugs to specific individuals to maximize blood pressure effects. Design, Setting, and Participants A randomized, double-blind, repeated crossover trial in men and women with grade 1 hypertension at low risk for cardiovascular events at an outpatient research clinic in Sweden. Mixed-effects models were used to assess the extent to which individuals responded better to one treatment than another and to estimate the additional blood pressure lowering achievable by personalized treatment. Interventions Each participant was scheduled for treatment in random order with 4 different classes of blood pressure–lowering drugs (lisinopril [angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor], candesartan [angiotensin-receptor blocker], hydrochlorothiazide [thiazide], and amlodipine [calcium channel blocker]), with repeated treatments for 2 classes. Main Outcomes and Measures Ambulatory daytime systolic blood pressure, measured at the end of each treatment period. Results There were 1468 completed treatment periods (median length, 56 days) recorded in 270 of the 280 randomized participants (54% men; mean age, 64 years). The blood pressure response to different treatments varied considerably between individuals ( P  < .001), specifically for the choices of lisinopril vs hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril vs amlodipine, candesartan vs hydrochlorothiazide, and candesartan vs amlodipine. Large differences were excluded for the choices of lisinopril vs candesartan and hydrochlorothiazide vs amlodipine. On average, personalized treatment had the potential to provide an additional 4.4 mm Hg–lower systolic blood pressure. Conclusions and Relevance These data reveal substantial heterogeneity in blood pressure response to drug therapy for hypertension, findings that may have implications for personalized therapy. The review did not provide a good estimate of the incidence of harms associated with ARBs because of the short duration of the trials and the lack of reporting of adverse effects in many of the trials. Plain language summary Angiotensin receptor blockers for the treatment of high blood pressure A class of drugs called angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) is commonly used to lower high blood pressure. This class includes drugs such as losartan (brand name: Cozaar), candesartan (Atacand), eprosartan (Teveten), irbesartan (Avapro), telmisartan (Micardis) and valsartan (Diovan). We asked how much this class of drugs lowers blood pressure and whether there is a difference between individual drugs within the class. The available scientific literature was searched to find all trials that had assessed these questions. We found 46 trials that randomly assigned participants to take either an ARB or an inert substance (placebo). These trials evaluated the BP lowering ability of 9 different ARBs in 13 451 participants altogether. The trials followed participants for only 7 weeks (though people are typically expected to take anti‐hypertension drugs for the rest of their lives). The blood pressure lowering effect was modest.  There was an 8‐point reduction in the upper number that signifies the systolic pressure and a 5‐point reduction in the lower number that signifies the diastolic pressure.  Most of the blood pressure lowering effect (about 70%) can be achieved with the lowest recommended dose of the drugs.  No ARB appears to be any better or worse than others in terms of blood pressure lowering ability. # D4-06 Claims check - biology part 1 (agent: claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-14)

## Summary

Checked 96 fact IDs: every fact named in the Digest and "What this suggests for the product" sections of D4-01, D4-03 and D4-05, plus D3-04-F09 for the GRAND clash. Each source was re-opened by a second route. Abstracts came from PubMed E-utilities efetch. Full texts came from Europe PMC fullTextXML, NCBI efetch db=pmc or the PMC article page. Labels came from the DailyMed SPL XML service (v2), and the guidelines from the KDIGO 2024 and ICMR NEDL PDFs, the NICE NG136 page and openFDA 510(k).

Counts: CONFIRMED 93, CORRECTED 2, CONTESTED 0, NOT FOUND 1.

The research notes recorded their sources faithfully. Every number in the six named checks matched the source. All OUR ARITHMETIC sums in D4-03 (F34, F57, F61, F62) and D4-01 (F49, F50, F21) hold when redone.

Corrections:
1. GRAND (D3-04-F09 CORRECTED; D4-03-F40 CONFIRMED). Both counts are right but measure different things. The study **enrolled 1,920** treated patients at 18 centres in 12 states (7 regions). Only **1,578 with valid clinic and home readings were analysed**, and every percentage is of the 1,578: 55.9% well controlled, 5.1% white-coat uncontrolled, 21.8% masked uncontrolled, 17.2% sustained uncontrolled, 77.7% vs 55.9% controlled. D3-04-F09 attaches these percentages to "1,920 treated patients", which is wrong. Published online 6 Nov 2026 (Hypertens Res). The 1,920 figure is the denominator of the companion knowledge paper (D4-03-F41).
2. D4-05-F11 (OUTREACH). 748 people (not 720) were excluded after visit 1, and 720 of them because they were adherent or their status was unconfirmed. This does not change a product rule.

Cautions that bear on product rules (the facts are recorded correctly, but these points limit their use):
- The "<10 mmHg fall after a drug is added" trigger (D4-05-F14) is Lane et al.'s rule for **ordering a confirmatory drug assay** in patients on 2 drugs. It is not a non-adherence classifier. At protocol step 3 (adding telmisartan 40 to amlodipine 10), the mean observed fall in the label trial was 11.1 mmHg, of which 3.7 beyond staying on amlodipine 10 (D4-01-F50). So many adherent patients will fall less than 10 mmHg, and the rule will flag them often.
- The "77% to 85% per added drug" figure (D4-05-F03) comes from an abstract that says "increase in nonadherence" without naming odds or risk; the full text could not be opened. It is per prescribed drug, not per dose step (steps 2 and 4 add no drug). The product line "risk rises about 1.8 times" turns odds into risk, and the Brazil figure is 1.57 (F07).
- The KDIGO 2024 recheck rule (D4-05-F27, F28) is quoted exactly. It is a **CKD** guideline practice point and says "depending on the current GFR and serum potassium". A >30% creatinine rise (PP 3.6.4) is not the same size as a >30% eGFR fall (PP 2.1.4).
- The noise bands in D4-03-F33/F34 come from **untreated** IDH participants (mean home BP 115/77). Treated older patients vary more (F10), so the 8.5 and 12.5 mmHg change thresholds are probably too narrow for the loop's patients.
- D4-03-F11/F61: 4.7 and 5.1 mmHg are the mixed model's **residual SD around each person's own fitted monthly trend**. The paper calls this "short-term intra-participant BP variability" and describes it as the SD of "any 1-week set" (HOMEBP) or of a calendar-month set (TASMINH4). It never says "SD of monthly means". The F61 sums hold, but its stated reason ("includes slow real drift") does not: each person's linear drift is already in the model.
- The seasonal figures are not home-cuff data. Punjab (D4-03-F31): trained nurses with a sphygmomanometer at home or the workplace, 9 am to 2 pm, mean of 2 readings 5 min apart, in a general community sample (hypertension prevalence 10% to 24%), not treated patients. Delhi (F32): readings at 4 investigator home visits in normotensive women aged 18 to 40.
- D4-01-F03: the "generally much larger" variation sentence is in PHYSIC's Introduction and cites earlier studies; it is not a PHYSIC result. PHYSIC's 4.4 mmHg is model-based ("assuming the fitted model to be true").

## Checks

| Fact ID | Claim as recorded | Verdict | What was found |
|---|---|---|---|
| D3-04-F09 | GRAND: 18 centres, 12 states, 1,920 treated patients; clinic-only control 77.7% vs 55.9%; masked uncontrolled 21.8%; white-coat 5.1%; sustained 17.2%; published 2026-11-06 | CORRECTED | 1,920 were enrolled; 1,578 with valid clinic and home BP were analysed, and every percentage is of 1,578. Centres, states, percentages and date (online 6 Nov 2026, Hypertens Res) all match. https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=42995223&rettype=abstract&retmode=text |
| D4-01-F01 | PHYSIC: 280 randomised (270 analysed, 1,468 periods); personalised choice 4.4 mmHg lower SBP than fixed choice; 3.1 vs lisinopril | CONFIRMED | Abstract: 280 randomised, 270 analysed, 1,468 periods, 54% men, mean age 64, 4.4 mmHg. Full text: 3.1 mmHg vs lisinopril, eTable 7. Both are model estimates ("assuming the fitted model to be true"). https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=37039792&rettype=abstract&retmode=text and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10091169/ |
| D4-01-F02 | PHYSIC: between-person differences for lisinopril or candesartan vs HCTZ or amlodipine; large differences excluded for lisinopril vs candesartan and HCTZ vs amlodipine | CONFIRMED | Abstract wording matches. The split is RAS blocker vs (amlodipine or thiazide). HCTZ and amlodipine are two different classes that behave alike, so "within families" means within these two pairs. # D4-06 Claims check - biology part 1 (agent: claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-14)

## Summary

Checked 96 fact IDs: every fact named in the Digest and "What this suggests for the product" sections of D4-01, D4-03 and D4-05, plus D3-04-F09 for the GRAND clash. Each source was re-opened by a second route. Abstracts came from PubMed E-utilities efetch. Full texts came from Europe PMC fullTextXML, NCBI efetch db=pmc or the PMC article page. Labels came from the DailyMed SPL XML service (v2), and the guidelines from the KDIGO 2024 and ICMR NEDL PDFs, the NICE NG136 page and openFDA 510(k).

Counts: CONFIRMED 93, CORRECTED 2, CONTESTED 0, NOT FOUND 1.

The research notes recorded their sources faithfully. Every number in the six named checks matched the source. All OUR ARITHMETIC sums in D4-03 (F34, F57, F61, F62) and D4-01 (F49, F50, F21) hold when redone.

Corrections:
1. GRAND (D3-04-F09 CORRECTED; D4-03-F40 CONFIRMED). Both counts are right but measure different things. The study **enrolled 1,920** treated patients at 18 centres in 12 states (7 regions). Only **1,578 with valid clinic and home readings were analysed**, and every percentage is of the 1,578: 55.9% well controlled, 5.1% white-coat uncontrolled, 21.8% masked uncontrolled, 17.2% sustained uncontrolled, 77.7% vs 55.9% controlled. D3-04-F09 attaches these percentages to "1,920 treated patients", which is wrong. Published online 6 Nov 2026 (Hypertens Res). The 1,920 figure is the denominator of the companion knowledge paper (D4-03-F41).
2. D4-05-F11 (OUTREACH). 748 people (not 720) were excluded after visit 1, and 720 of them because they were adherent or their status was unconfirmed. This does not change a product rule.

Cautions that bear on product rules (the facts are recorded correctly, but these points limit their use):
- The "<10 mmHg fall after a drug is added" trigger (D4-05-F14) is Lane et al.'s rule for **ordering a confirmatory drug assay** in patients on 2 drugs. It is not a non-adherence classifier. At protocol step 3 (adding telmisartan 40 to amlodipine 10), the mean observed fall in the label trial was 11.1 mmHg, of which 3.7 beyond staying on amlodipine 10 (D4-01-F50). So many adherent patients will fall less than 10 mmHg, and the rule will flag them often.
- The "77% to 85% per added drug" figure (D4-05-F03) comes from an abstract that says "increase in nonadherence" without naming odds or risk; the full text could not be opened. It is per prescribed drug, not per dose step (steps 2 and 4 add no drug). The product line "risk rises about 1.8 times" turns odds into risk, and the Brazil figure is 1.57 (F07).
- The KDIGO 2024 recheck rule (D4-05-F27, F28) is quoted exactly. It is a **CKD** guideline practice point and says "depending on the current GFR and serum potassium". A >30% creatinine rise (PP 3.6.4) is not the same size as a >30% eGFR fall (PP 2.1.4).
- The noise bands in D4-03-F33/F34 come from **untreated** IDH participants (mean home BP 115/77). Treated older patients vary more (F10), so the 8.5 and 12.5 mmHg change thresholds are probably too narrow for the loop's patients.
- D4-03-F11/F61: 4.7 and 5.1 mmHg are the mixed model's **residual SD around each person's own fitted monthly trend**. The paper calls this "short-term intra-participant BP variability" and describes it as the SD of "any 1-week set" (HOMEBP) or of a calendar-month set (TASMINH4). It never says "SD of monthly means". The F61 sums hold, but its stated reason ("includes slow real drift") does not: each person's linear drift is already in the model.
- The seasonal figures are not home-cuff data. Punjab (D4-03-F31): trained nurses with a sphygmomanometer at home or the workplace, 9 am to 2 pm, mean of 2 readings 5 min apart, in a general community sample (hypertension prevalence 10% to 24%), not treated patients. Delhi (F32): readings at 4 investigator home visits in normotensive women aged 18 to 40.
- D4-01-F03: the "generally much larger" variation sentence is in PHYSIC's Introduction and cites earlier studies; it is not a PHYSIC result. PHYSIC's 4.4 mmHg is model-based ("assuming the fitted model to be true").

I re-checked 96 facts and wrote the claims-check note. The three notes recorded their sources faithfully: 93 CONFIRMED, 2 CORRECTED, 0 CONTESTED, 1 NOT FOUND. The table has 96 rows, one fact ID per row, and passes a format check (5 pipes per row, no duplicate IDs). The research notes were not edited.

The 96 are every fact in the Digest and product sections of D4-01, D4-03 and D4-05, plus D3-04-F09. That is about twice your estimate, because the Digests name many facts. Every source was re-opened by a second route: PubMed efetch, Europe PMC full text, PMC pages, DailyMed label XML, the KDIGO 2024 and ICMR NEDL PDFs, NICE NG136 and openFDA. Searches used: 0 web searches.

**CORRECTED**
1. **D3-04-F09 (GRAND).** Both counts are right but measure different things. 1,920 treated patients were enrolled (18 centres, 12 states, 7 regions); only 1,578 with valid clinic and home readings were analysed. Every percentage is of the 1,578: 77.7% vs 55.9% controlled, 21.8% masked uncontrolled, 5.1% white-coat, 17.2% sustained. D3-04-F09 wrongly attaches them to 1,920. Published online 6 Nov 2026. D4-03-F40 is CONFIRMED as recorded.
2. **D4-05-F11 (OUTREACH).** 748 people were excluded after visit 1, not 720; 720 of the 748 were excluded because they were adherent or unconfirmed. No product rule changes.

**NOT FOUND**
- **D4-05-F36** (NT-proBNP price, ₹1,200 to ₹3,520) is from search snippets only. I did not re-open it, so it stays SNIPPET.

**Your six checks: all confirmed, with caveats**
- **GRAND:** resolved as above.
- **Telmisartan/amlodipine label:** 947 patients, 3.7 vs 3.9 mmHg, and oedema 4.3% vs 27.2% in 1,097 all match. So does every factorial value, and the step sums of 5.3, 4.0 and 1.7 mmHg hold. Amlodipine oedema is 3.0% vs 10.8%, and 5.6% in men vs 14.6% in women.
- **PHYSIC:**
  - 4.4 mmHg in 280 randomised (270 analysed) and 3.1 mmHg vs lisinopril match. Both are model estimates.
  - The differences are between a renin-angiotensin blocker and amlodipine or the thiazide, not within those pairs. Amlodipine and the thiazide are two different classes that behave alike. Large within-pair differences were "excluded", which is not the same as zero.
  - The "natural variation is much larger than a titration step" sentence is from the paper's introduction, citing older studies. It is not a PHYSIC result.
- **Noise figures:**
  - The 6.37 and 4.36 mmHg SDs (3-day and 7-day means) and the 4.7 and 5.1 month-to-month figures match.
  - Every OUR ARITHMETIC sum holds (F34, F57, F61, F62, and the D4-01 sums).
  - 4.7 and 5.1 are the model's leftover scatter around each person's own monthly trend. The paper never calls this "SD across monthly means", so the F61 sums hold but its stated reason ("includes slow drift") does not.
  - The 6.37 and 4.36 come from untreated young people with mean home BP 115/77. The 8.5 and 12.5 mmHg change thresholds are probably too narrow for older treated patients.
- **Seasonal figures:**
  - 9.01/5.61 Punjab and 11.07/6.79 Delhi match.
  - None are home-cuff readings. Punjab: trained nurses with a mercury-type cuff at home or work, 9 am to 2 pm, mean of 2 readings, in a general community sample. Delhi: investigator home visits, normotensive women aged 18 to 40.
- **D4-05 checks:**
  - 31.2% pooled non-adherence matches. 77% and 85% match, but the abstract says "increase in nonadherence" without saying odds or risk, and the figure is per prescribed drug, not per dose step.
  - The KDIGO 2024 rule is verbatim (recheck within 2 to 4 weeks; continue unless creatinine rises more than 30% within 4 weeks). It comes from a kidney-disease guideline and applies "depending on the current GFR and serum potassium".
  - Amlodipine: no significant heart-rate change, +0.3 bpm in angina trials. Telmisartan: "no changes in the heart rate".
  - The "<10 mmHg" rule is quoted correctly from Lane et al.

**Cautions that bear on product rules**
- **The "<10 mmHg fall" flag** is a trigger to order a confirmatory drug assay in patients on two drugs, not a sign of non-adherence. At step 3 (adding telmisartan 40 to amlodipine 10), the mean observed fall in the label trial was 11.1 mmHg. Many adherent patients will fall less than 10 and be flagged.
- **"Risk rises about 1.8 times per added drug"** turns odds into risk, and the Brazil figure is 1.57. Steps 2 and 4 are dose increases and add no drug.

Not re-opened: facts outside the Digest and product sections (listed in the note), the CPIC/GRK4 and Swissmedic sentences in D4-01-F36, and the SNIPPET price facts.

- D4-06 Claims check - biology part 1.md

- **"Risk rises about 1.8 times per added drug"** turns odds into risk, and the Brazil figure is 1.57. Steps 2 and 4 are dose increases and add no drug.
